# To The Max, full reference

> To The Max is a one-operator marketing agency in Huntsville, Alabama running Meta ads, landing pages, and lead follow-up for local service businesses.

Last updated: 2026-09-22
Source: https://tothemax.marketing/

===============================================================================
ABOUT
===============================================================================

Q: What does To The Max do?
A: To The Max builds and runs the whole lead system for a local business: the Meta ads, the landing page the ads point at, the form that captures the lead, and the follow-up that reaches them before the lead goes cold. It ships as one connected system, because an ad without a converting page and fast follow-up behind it is money on fire.

Q: Who runs the agency?
A: Maximus Fayrweather, and only Maximus Fayrweather. It is a one-operator agency by design. You text the founder and the founder answers, usually the same day. There is no account manager between you and the person running your campaigns.

Q: Where is To The Max based and who does it work with?
A: Huntsville, Alabama. Clients are local and owner-operated service businesses: home services, trades, shops, studios, and practices that win work in their own city. The work is done remotely, so the client does not have to be in Huntsville, but the marketing is always built for a business that sells in a specific place.

Q: Why would you trust a young agency?
A: Because the founder is his own first client. Maximus owns Supreme Clean, a pressure washing company in Huntsville doing five thousand dollars a month, and every ad dollar behind it is his own. Strategies are paid for and tested there before they are ever sold. When one fails, he pays for that lesson instead of a client.

Q: What does it cost?
A: Services are packaged, not itemised. Package one is Meta ads plus the CRM and follow-up system. Package two adds Google. A website is included in both and is never a separate line item. An AI receptionist is sold separately because it solves a different problem. You see the exact number, and the expected cost per lead, in writing before you spend anything.

Q: Who owns the ad account and the leads?
A: You do, from day one. Every ad account, page, creative asset, and lead belongs to the client. If the relationship ends, nothing has to be handed back because it was never taken. Agencies that hold the account are holding a hostage, and that is not how this one works.

Q: How long is the commitment?
A: Month to month. There is no six or twelve month contract. The work has to be worth renewing every month, which is a harder standard for the agency and a safer one for the client.

Q: What results can you actually show?
A: Whatever is in the Ledger on the proof page, and nothing else. Every entry is dated and the numbers are real. There are no borrowed client logos, no invented star ratings, and no testimonials from people who do not exist. The record is short because the agency is young, and it grows every week.

Q: How do I start?
A: Text or call 281-908-4874 for a fifteen minute conversation with no pitch in it. If the business is not a fit, you get told so on the call and pointed somewhere better. If it is, you get the plan in writing, including the budget and what a lead should cost you, before a dollar is spent.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ARTISTS AND COMMISSION STUDIOS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/artists-and-studios

This is the one category on this site where a client campaign is already live and documented. Sophi Paints signed in July 2026 and had a full funnel and a Meta lead campaign running inside two weeks. The dates are in the Ledger.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Artists are told to build an audience and wait. That is a five year plan for a business that needs commissions this quarter.
- Commissioned work is a considered, emotional, high-ticket purchase with no urgency attached to it, so without a reason to act now the lead sits forever.
- Most artists have no capture mechanism at all. The work gets admired, shared, and saved, and no contact detail is ever collected.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A real offer with a boundary: a discount for the first few commissions, a seasonal deadline, or a limited number of slots, so the decision has a date on it.
- Lead forms that capture the subject, the occasion, and the timeline, because a commission quote is impossible without them.
- Portfolio-led creative using finished pieces, in the style and subject you actually want more of.
- Follow-up that survives a slow, emotional decision, since a commission can take weeks to commit to and the enquiry going quiet is not a no.
- Occasion-driven campaigns around holidays, graduations, memorials, and weddings, which is where commission demand actually concentrates.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Pet or family portrait: $300 to $1,200
- Mural or large commission: $1,500 to $8,000
- What a commission lead can cost: $15 to $60
- Decision window to plan for: 2 to 6 weeks
- Where demand concentrates: Holidays and occasions
Note: Documented client work in this category is on the proof page, dated. The ranges above are planning numbers, not results.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for artists?
A: Yes, for commissioned work specifically, because the decision is emotional and the imagery does the selling. What most artists lack is not reach but an offer with a deadline and a way to capture contact details. The work gets admired and saved, and nobody ever asks for a name.

Q: How much does an art commission lead cost?
A: Fifteen to sixty dollars in most markets. Against a portrait commission of several hundred to a thousand dollars, that is comfortable even at a modest close rate. The constraint is usually studio capacity rather than lead cost.

Q: What should an artist's ad offer?
A: Something with a boundary. A discount on the first few commissions, a limited number of slots before a holiday deadline, or a seasonal package. Commissioned art has no natural urgency, so the offer has to supply it or the enquiry sits in a drafts folder forever.

Q: When is the best time to advertise commissioned art?
A: Around occasions. Christmas, Mother's Day, graduations, weddings, and memorials are when people actually commission personal work, and the lead time means the campaign has to run four to eight weeks ahead of the date, not during the week of it.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AUTO DETAILING SHOPS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/auto-detailing-shops

Detailing has the most beautiful creative in local service and the worst offers. Everybody posts a satisfying paint correction clip. Almost nobody attaches a package, a price, and a bookable slot to it.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- A gorgeous reel with no offer is entertainment. It gets saved, it gets shared, and it books nothing, because the viewer was never told what to do or what it costs.
- Detailers train their own customers to wait for a discount. Run a half-price special every month and the full-price package stops existing, because the market learns your real price is the sale price.
- The ceramic coating customer and the twenty dollar wash customer are not the same person and do not respond to the same ad. Most shops run one campaign at both and get the cheap one.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Three named packages with real prices, so the ad has something to close on instead of ending at a direct message.
- Coating and correction run as their own campaign into higher-value vehicle audiences, kept away from the entry-level wash creative that would eat the budget.
- Booking straight into a calendar slot, not a conversation. Every message thread between the ad and the appointment is a place the customer leaves.
- A maintenance plan offered at pickup, because a detailed car needs upkeep and a recurring customer is worth ten times the one-off.
- Before and after on cars that look like the target customer's car. A corrected supercar sells nothing to the person driving a three-year-old SUV.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Full interior and exterior detail: $200 to $500
- Paint correction and ceramic coating: $900 to $2,500
- What a detail lead can cost: $15 to $45
- What a coating lead can cost: $50 to $150
- The quiet win: Recurring maintenance plans
Note: Mobile detailers should add drive time to the cost of every job before deciding what a lead can cost. A route that looks profitable on ticket alone often is not.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for auto detailing?
A: Yes, because the results are visual and the before and after does the selling for you. What stops most detailers is that the ad ends in a conversation instead of a booking. Attach a named package, a real price, and a calendar link, and the same creative starts producing appointments.

Q: How much does an auto detailing lead cost?
A: Fifteen to forty-five dollars for standard detailing and fifty to one hundred and fifty for ceramic coating work. The coating lead looks expensive until you put it against a fifteen hundred dollar ticket, at which point it is the best buy in the shop.

Q: Should detailers run discounts?
A: Sparingly, and never on a schedule. A monthly special teaches the market that your real price is the discount, and the full-price package quietly dies. Use a bundle, a free add-on, or a limited number of slots at a named date instead. Same urgency, no damage to the price.

Q: How do you sell ceramic coating with ads?
A: As a separate campaign with its own creative, aimed at newer and higher-value vehicles, selling protection and resale value rather than shine. Coating creative mixed into a wash campaign loses every auction to the cheaper offer, so it never gets a real test and the shop concludes coating does not sell.

Q: Is mobile detailing harder to advertise than a shop?
A: It is different math, not harder. Mobile has no location to draw people to, so the targeting radius and drive time have to be priced into every job before you decide what a lead can cost. Tight radius, higher minimum ticket, and route-clustered scheduling are what make mobile work.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AUTO REPAIR SHOPS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/auto-repair-shops

An independent shop is not competing on price with the dealership. It is competing on trust with every other independent shop in a five mile radius, and the customer picks one and stays for a decade.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Coupon advertising buys the customer who will leave for the next coupon. An oil change special with nothing behind it is the most expensive customer in the shop.
- The real prize is the customer who switches away from the dealership permanently, and that is a trust decision, not a discount decision.
- Most shops never contact a customer again after the repair, which means the entire value of the relationship depends on the customer remembering them, which they do not.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- An entry offer tied to a real inspection, so the first visit surfaces actual work instead of just discounting a service you already do cheaply.
- Trust as the creative: named technicians, certifications, warranty terms, and the shop itself, because the customer is choosing who to believe.
- Service reminders and follow-up that keep the shop in front of the customer between visits, which is where the lifetime value actually comes from.
- Specialty campaigns where you have a real advantage, whether that is a brand, diagnostics, fleet work, or transmissions, since specialists beat generalists in the feed.
- Fleet and small business campaigns, which produce steady, scheduled, higher-margin work with no competition in the feed.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Average repair ticket: $300 to $900
- Annual value of a retained customer: $800 to $2,000
- What a new customer can cost: $30 to $90
- Visits before a customer is loyal: 2 to 3
- The real product: Being their shop
Note: The second visit is the one that matters. A campaign that produces first visits and no second visits is buying customers for somebody else.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for auto repair shops?
A: Yes, for winning customers away from dealerships and building a local reputation, both of which are trust decisions the feed handles well. They work poorly for roadside emergencies, where the driver is searching from the side of the road and picking whoever is closest and open.

Q: How much should an auto repair shop pay for a new customer?
A: Thirty to ninety dollars is reasonable when a retained customer is worth a thousand a year or more. The number that decides the campaign is not the first visit, it is the second. A first visit with no return is a customer you paid to send somewhere else.

Q: Should an auto shop run oil change specials?
A: Only as a doorway to a real inspection. A standalone cheap oil change buys a customer who leaves for the next coupon. Tied to a multi-point inspection that surfaces genuine work and starts a real conversation, the same offer builds a customer who stays for years.

Q: How do independent shops compete with dealerships?
A: On trust and on the relationship, not on price. Named technicians, visible certifications, a stated warranty, and honest explanations of what does and does not need doing are what move a customer off a dealership. That message works far better in a feed than in a search result.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHIROPRACTIC PRACTICES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/chiropractors

Chiropractic advertising lives or dies on one number almost nobody tracks: the percentage of booked new patients who actually walk through the door. Everything else is downstream of it.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- A cheap new patient offer produces a full calendar and an empty waiting room, because people who paid nothing feel nothing about missing an appointment.
- Health is a sensitive advertising category. Copy that names the reader's pain or condition gets rejected and can put the ad account at risk, and most chiropractic copy is written exactly that way.
- The practice makes money on care plans, not first visits, and most advertising stops thinking at the booking.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A paid or committed first visit rather than a free one, because a small payment is the single largest lever on show rate in this category.
- Copy written against Meta's health policy from the first draft, in the third person, about the care rather than the reader's body.
- Confirmation and reminder sequences between booking and appointment, which is where most of the no-shows are actually lost.
- Condition-specific campaigns where policy allows, since the message that works for a car accident is not the message that works for desk posture.
- Care plan conversion tracked as the real outcome, because a practice built on first visits alone is running a treadmill.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- First visit offer: $29 to $99
- Care plan value: $1,500 to $4,000
- What a booked new patient can cost: $40 to $120
- Show rate to defend: 70% or better
- The only outcome that counts: Patients on a plan
Note: A forty dollar lead with a forty percent show rate is a hundred dollar patient. A hundred dollar lead with an eighty percent show rate is a hundred and twenty-five dollar patient and a better one. Show rate beats lead price every time.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for chiropractors?
A: Yes, and it remains one of the most reliable local health categories, as long as the copy is compliant and the offer produces people who actually show up. The failure is almost never traffic. It is a free offer that fills a calendar with no-shows and a practice that never tracks the difference.

Q: Why do chiropractic ads get rejected?
A: Personal attributes. Copy addressed to the reader's back, neck, pain, or posture implies a personal health condition, which Meta's policy prohibits. Writing about the care and the outcome in the third person clears review reliably and performs just as well.

Q: Should a chiropractor offer a free first visit?
A: No. A small paid first visit dramatically improves show rate, because a free appointment is worth nothing and gets treated accordingly. Twenty-nine to ninety-nine dollars costs you almost no lead volume and roughly doubles the number of people who actually arrive.

Q: How much should a chiropractic new patient cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and twenty dollars per booked appointment, judged alongside show rate. Against a care plan worth a few thousand dollars, even the high end is comfortable. The practice that wins is the one measuring patients on plans, not bookings on a calendar.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CONCRETE AND EPOXY FLOORING CONTRACTORS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/concrete-and-epoxy-contractors

Concrete and epoxy sell the same way kitchens do: on a photograph and a price range. The contractors who win in the feed are the ones who show the finished floor and state the starting number.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Every quote request that arrives without a budget expectation is a site visit you may not get paid for. Unqualified leads in this trade do not cost money, they cost days.
- Decorative and epoxy work is highly visual and most contractors advertise it with a photo of a truck. The finished garage floor, the stamped patio, the polished showroom floor is the ad.
- Commercial and industrial coating work is steadier and larger than residential, and it is almost invisible in local advertising because everyone is chasing homeowners.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Qualification in the form: square footage, current surface condition, timeline, and a budget band. Three extra questions save a week of driving.
- Finished-work photography as the entire creative direction, shot in the kind of property your best customers own.
- A stated starting price per square foot, which loses the tyre kickers on purpose and raises the quality of everything that comes through.
- A separate commercial and industrial campaign for warehouses, shops, and showrooms, where jobs are bigger and competition in the feed is thin.
- Follow-up built for a long window, because a decorative floor is often decided across a whole season of home projects.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Residential garage epoxy: $2,000 to $6,000
- Stamped or decorative patio: $4,000 to $15,000
- Commercial coating job: $10,000 to $80,000
- What a qualified lead can cost: $80 to $250
- Decision window to plan for: 3 to 10 weeks
Note: The cost that matters here is not per lead, it is per site visit that turns into a contract. An unqualified lead costs a half day of your time, which is worth more than the lead fee.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for concrete and epoxy contractors?
A: Yes, because the product is intensely visual and the ticket is high enough to absorb a meaningful lead cost. A photograph of a finished garage floor or stamped patio in a house like the viewer's does more selling than any amount of copy about the material.

Q: How much does a concrete or epoxy lead cost?
A: Eighty to two hundred and fifty dollars for a qualified lead. That is fine on a four thousand dollar garage floor. What is not fine is a cheap lead that produces an unpaid site visit, because in this trade your time is the expensive input, not the lead fee.

Q: Should the ad include a price?
A: A starting price per square foot, yes. It will reduce your lead volume, which is the point. Every lead who leaves because of the number was a site visit you were never going to be paid for, and the ones who remain arrive already expecting a real conversation.

Q: How do you qualify concrete leads before the site visit?
A: Ask three questions in the form: square footage, the condition of the existing surface, and when they want it done. Add a budget band if your average ticket is high. Those questions take ten seconds to answer and save entire days of driving to quotes that were never going to happen.

Q: Is commercial epoxy work worth advertising?
A: It is usually the best part of the business. Warehouses, workshops, showrooms, and commercial kitchens all need coatings, the jobs are several times larger than residential, and virtually no contractor is running ads at that buyer. The auction is close to empty.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DENTAL PRACTICES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/dental-practices

A dental practice does not need more patients. It needs more of the right cases. Those are two completely different campaigns, and the cheap new-patient special usually buys the wrong one.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- The ninety-nine dollar cleaning and x-ray special fills the schedule with patients who came for the special, decline treatment, and leave. It is a busy calendar and a flat bank account.
- High-value cases, implants, full arch, ortho, cosmetic, are slow and emotional decisions. They need months of follow-up, and most practices give up after two voicemails.
- Dental is a sensitive advertising category in the same way aesthetics is. Copy that names the viewer's teeth or appearance gets rejected, and most dental ad copy is written exactly that way.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Case-type campaigns first: implants, clear aligners, full arch, cosmetic. Each gets its own creative, its own audience, and its own budget line.
- A consultation offer with a stated scan, a stated plan, and a stated price range, so the appointment produces a decision rather than a maybe.
- Follow-up measured in months, not days, with the front desk given an actual sequence. High-value dental leads convert on the fifth touch far more often than the first.
- Compliant copy written against Meta's health policy from the first draft, third person, about the treatment rather than the reader's mouth.
- Reactivation of dormant patients in the practice management system, which almost always books more chair time in the first month than new advertising does.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Single implant case: $3,000 to $6,000
- Full arch case: $20,000 to $50,000
- Clear aligner case: $3,500 to $7,000
- What a high-value consult lead can cost: $100 to $400
- Touches before a big case closes: Often 5 or more
Note: On a full arch case, a four hundred dollar lead at a one in ten close rate still means four thousand dollars of ad spend on a job worth many times that. The cheap new-patient lead is the expensive one.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for dentists?
A: Yes, particularly for high-value elective cases: implants, clear aligners, full arch, and cosmetic work. Those are considered, emotional purchases that respond well to feed advertising. Routine hygiene is better served by search and by reactivating the patients already in your system.

Q: How much does a dental implant lead cost?
A: One hundred to four hundred dollars for a consultation booking. That sounds high until you put it against a case worth several thousand dollars. On full arch, even a four hundred dollar lead closing at one in ten is comfortable. Cost per case is the only number worth reporting.

Q: Should a dental practice run a new-patient special?
A: Only if you want a full schedule and a flat bank account. Cheap cleaning specials attract patients who came for the price and decline treatment. If you run one, it should be tied to a comprehensive exam that surfaces real treatment, not to a standalone discount.

Q: Why do dental ads get rejected on Facebook?
A: Personal attributes, nearly every time. Copy addressed to the reader's teeth, smile, or appearance reads as implying a personal condition and violates Meta's health policy. Writing about the procedure and the outcome in the third person clears review and performs no worse.

Q: What is the fastest way for a dentist to fill the schedule?
A: Reactivate dormant patients. Most practices have hundreds of people with unscheduled treatment plans or overdue hygiene sitting in the practice management software. A specific, dated message about the treatment they already agreed to books chair time within a week and costs nothing in ad spend.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ELECTRICAL CONTRACTORS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/electricians

Electrical is the trade most often stuck selling hours. The companies that get out of that trap advertise projects instead: panels, generators, EV chargers, lighting. Same crew, same van, different business.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- An hourly service call is the lowest form of electrical revenue and the hardest to advertise profitably, because there is no headline in it. Nobody stops scrolling for an hourly rate.
- The project work has obvious triggers that almost nobody advertises against. A new EV in the driveway. A panel too small for a remodel. A neighbourhood that lost power for three days last winter and is now shopping generators.
- Electricians are chronically undersold on trust signals. Licence, insurance, permit handling, and inspection pass rate are exactly what a homeowner is nervous about, and they almost never appear in the ad.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Project campaigns instead of service campaigns: panel upgrades, EV charger installs, whole-home generators, recessed and landscape lighting.
- Trigger timing. Generator campaigns after an outage event, EV charger campaigns into new-EV-owning audiences, panel campaigns into older housing stock.
- Licence, insurance, and permit handling stated plainly in the creative, because that is the actual objection in a trade where bad work burns a house down.
- A commercial and property-manager campaign running alongside, since recurring commercial maintenance is the steadiest revenue in the trade and is barely contested in the feed.
- Follow-up that survives a long decision. A panel upgrade can take six weeks to decide, and a lead that goes quiet is not a lead that said no.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Panel upgrade: $1,800 to $4,500
- EV charger install: $600 to $2,200
- Whole-home generator: $8,000 to $18,000
- What a project lead can cost: $50 to $200
- Decision window to plan for: 2 to 8 weeks
Note: The long decision window is the thing most electricians get wrong. Judging a panel or generator campaign after ten days will make you kill something that was about to pay for itself.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for electricians?
A: For project work, clearly yes: panel upgrades, EV chargers, generators, and lighting all sell well in the feed because they are visual, high ticket, and considered. For hourly service calls the math is thin, because there is no compelling offer to put in front of someone who does not currently have a problem.

Q: What should an electrician advertise?
A: Projects with a picture and a price range: panel upgrades, EV charger installation, whole-home generators, recessed lighting, and landscape lighting. Each has a visible trigger you can target against. An hourly rate has no trigger and no image, which is why service-call ads underperform in this trade.

Q: How much does an electrical lead cost?
A: Fifty to two hundred dollars for project work. On a three thousand dollar panel upgrade closing at one in three, a hundred and fifty dollar lead is comfortable. The number that matters is cost per booked project, and in this trade that can look bad for three weeks and fine at week six.

Q: Are EV charger installs worth advertising?
A: Yes, because the trigger is dated and targetable. Somebody who just bought an electric vehicle needs a charger within weeks and usually does not know who to call. The ticket is modest but the customer is now yours for the panel upgrade, the generator, and everything else in the house.

Q: How long should you wait before judging an electrical campaign?
A: At least six weeks on project work. Panels and generators carry a two to eight week decision window, so a campaign judged at day ten looks like a failure and is usually about to convert. This is the single most common reason electricians switch off a campaign that was working.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FENCE AND DECK BUILDERS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/fence-and-deck-companies

Fences and decks are bought in the spring and decided in the winter. Companies that only advertise when the phone is already ringing are paying the highest possible price for work they would have got anyway.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- The season compresses demand into a few months, and everyone bids for the same attention at the same time, at the worst possible cost.
- Fence and deck leads arrive with wildly different scopes. A sixty foot privacy fence and a full multi-level deck are not the same conversation, and an unqualified form treats them as if they were.
- The trigger events, a new dog, a new pool, a new baby, a fence that finally fell over, are all targetable and almost never targeted.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Off-season campaigns that book the spring calendar in advance at a fraction of in-season lead costs.
- Material and linear footage captured in the form, so the estimate is a real number rather than another discovery call.
- Finished-project photography in yards that resemble the customer's, since this is bought entirely on the picture of the outcome.
- Trigger-based campaigns around new pets, new pools, and new homes, where the need is immediate and the competition is not looking.
- Financing shown for larger decks, which moves a twelve thousand dollar project into a monthly figure people can act on.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Privacy fence: $3,000 to $10,000
- Deck build: $8,000 to $25,000
- Repair and restaining: $800 to $3,000
- What a qualified lead can cost: $60 to $200
- When to book spring: January and February
Note: Lead costs in this trade can be half in February what they are in May, for work delivered in the same season. Booking early is the single highest-return decision in the category.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for fence and deck companies?
A: Yes, because outdoor projects are visual, high ticket, and driven by clear life triggers. The highest-return version is running them in the off-season to book the spring calendar, when lead costs are a fraction of what everyone else pays in May.

Q: When should a fence company start advertising for spring?
A: January and February. Homeowners plan outdoor projects months ahead, and lead costs in winter are often half the spring rate for work delivered in the same season. By the time the phone is ringing on its own, you are paying peak prices for demand you already had.

Q: How much does a fence or deck lead cost?
A: Sixty to two hundred dollars for a qualified lead. On a six thousand dollar fence closing at one in three, that is comfortable. Capture linear footage and material in the form, because scope varies so wildly in this trade that an unqualified lead is barely a lead at all.

Q: What triggers a fence purchase?
A: A new dog, a new pool, a new baby, a new house, or a fence that finally came down in a storm. Every one of those is targetable and almost nobody targets them, which makes those audiences some of the cheapest high-intent attention available in the trade.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GARAGE DOOR COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/garage-door-companies

A broken garage door is an emergency and a new garage door is a curb appeal purchase. They are opposite ends of the same business and they need opposite advertising.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Repair demand is urgent and search-driven, and trying to win it in the feed means bidding on a broken spring that has not broken yet.
- Replacement is a curb appeal purchase with a real ticket, and it is highly visual, and almost every garage door ad shows a truck instead of a door.
- Openers, springs, and smart upgrades are easy, profitable add-ons and almost nobody advertises them as their own offer.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Replacement as the feed campaign, built on before and after curb appeal photography of actual houses in your market.
- Repair handled with speed: instant text back, a call inside minutes, and a same-day promise you can genuinely keep.
- A separate opener and smart upgrade campaign, which is a low-friction entry point and a profitable one.
- Targeting on housing stock age, since a twenty-year-old subdivision is a neighbourhood full of failing doors and dated panels.
- Financing shown on premium doors, which moves a four thousand dollar decision into a monthly number.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Spring or opener repair: $150 to $600
- New door install: $1,200 to $5,000
- Smart opener upgrade: $400 to $900
- What a replacement lead can cost: $40 to $150
- What wins the repair job: Answering first
Note: Repair customers call three companies and hire the one that answers. Replacement customers take weeks and hire the one whose door they liked. Two different campaigns, two different follow-up rhythms.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for garage door companies?
A: Yes, for replacement and upgrades, which are visual curb appeal purchases with a real ticket. For emergency repair the feed is the wrong channel, because a homeowner with a broken spring is on Google right now. Run Meta for replacement and let search catch the breakdowns.

Q: How much does a garage door lead cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and fifty dollars for replacement leads. On a three thousand dollar install closing at one in three, that is comfortable. Repair leads are cheaper and convert on speed alone, which means the follow-up process matters more than the ad.

Q: What should a garage door ad show?
A: The door, on a house that looks like the customer's, ideally as a before and after. A new garage door is one of the largest visual changes to a home's front elevation, and that transformation is the entire pitch. A photo of your truck sells nothing.

Q: How do you sell garage door openers and upgrades?
A: As their own campaign. Smart openers, keypads, and battery backups are low-friction purchases with good margin, and they put a technician in a garage where an aging door gets noticed and quoted. Inside a replacement campaign they never get budget.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GUTTER INSTALLATION AND CLEANING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/gutter-companies

Gutters are the most weather-triggered purchase in home services. The companies that win are not the ones with better ads, they are the ones already running when the first heavy rain hits.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Demand arrives in spikes tied to weather and leaf drop, and most gutter companies start advertising after the spike, when costs are highest and the calendar is already going to fill anyway.
- Cleaning is a small ticket and installation and guards are a large one, and running them in the same campaign guarantees the cheap work eats the budget.
- Gutter guards are one of the few local products with a genuine long-term payback story, and almost nobody makes that argument in the ad.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Seasonal campaigns that switch on ahead of leaf drop and ahead of the rainy season, not during them.
- Cleaning and installation split into separate campaigns with separate budgets, because a two hundred dollar clean and a three thousand dollar install cannot share an optimisation target.
- A guard campaign built on the payback argument: the cost of never cleaning again against the cost of cleaning twice a year forever.
- Damage-trigger creative after heavy weather, aimed at the neighbourhoods that actually got hit.
- Cleaning customers moved onto a recurring schedule at the visit, which converts the cheapest lead in the trade into a repeating one.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Gutter cleaning: $150 to $400
- Full gutter replacement: $1,500 to $4,500
- Gutter guard install: $2,000 to $6,000
- What an install lead can cost: $50 to $180
- When to be live: Before leaf drop, before the rain
Note: The cleaning campaign rarely pays for itself on the clean alone. It pays when the technician on the roof books the guard install, so the two campaigns have to be judged together.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for gutter companies?
A: Yes, especially for guards and full replacement, which carry real tickets and a clear payback argument. Cleaning alone is a thin margin against a lead cost, so it works best as an entry point that puts a technician on the roof where the install gets sold.

Q: When should gutter ads run?
A: Ahead of the triggers, not during them. Live before leaf drop in autumn and before the rainy season in spring. Once the gutters are already overflowing, every competitor is bidding, costs spike, and the calendar was going to fill anyway.

Q: How do you sell gutter guards with ads?
A: With the payback maths. Two cleanings a year forever against a one-time install is an argument a homeowner can actually check, and it beats any feature list about mesh design. Show the number, show the timeline, and let them do the arithmetic themselves.

Q: Should gutter cleaning and installation share a campaign?
A: No. A two hundred dollar cleaning lead and a three thousand dollar install lead cannot share an optimisation target, and the algorithm will always find you more of the cheap one. Separate campaigns, separate budgets, judged together at the end of the month.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GYMS AND FITNESS STUDIOS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/gyms-and-fitness-studios

A gym is a subscription business wearing a building. Every advertising decision should be made against what a member is worth over their whole stay, and almost none of them are.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Free trial campaigns produce enormous lead volume and terrible members. Something free is worth nothing and gets treated accordingly, which is why the show rate on free trials is dismal.
- The January rush is a trap. A gym that acquires its whole year in six weeks has a churn cliff in March and no plan for it.
- Almost every gym measures cost per lead and stops there, which hides the only number that matters: what it costs to acquire a member who is still there in month six.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A paid trial or challenge instead of a free one. A small amount of money changes the show rate more than any other single lever in this category.
- Follow-up built for a decision people make with their ego. Speed matters, but so does a sequence that survives the week they decided to start Monday and did not.
- Offers matched to your actual model. A twenty-four hour access gym, a boutique studio, and a personal training business are three different businesses and cannot share one campaign.
- Retention treated as marketing. A member who stays nine months instead of four doubles what you can afford to pay for the next one.
- Community and results content as the creative, using real members with permission, because a stranger deciding on a gym is deciding whether they will fit in there.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Monthly membership: $40 to $200
- Average member lifetime: 4 to 14 months
- What a trial lead can cost: $15 to $50
- Acceptable cost per joined member: 1 to 2 months of dues
- The number nobody tracks: Trial show rate
Note: Cost per lead is a vanity metric in this category. The real one is cost per member still paying in month six, and it is often triple what the lead report suggests.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for gyms?
A: Yes, and gyms are one of the strongest local categories for it, because the decision is emotional, visual, and geographically bounded. The reason gym campaigns fail is almost never targeting. It is a free offer that produces leads who never show up and a follow-up process that stops after one call.

Q: How much should a gym pay per member?
A: One to two months of dues is a healthy acquisition cost, which at a hundred dollar membership means one to two hundred dollars per joined member. Cost per lead is a distraction. Measure cost per member still paying in month six, because that is the person who actually funds the gym.

Q: Are free trials or paid trials better for gym ads?
A: Paid, almost always. A free trial produces far more leads and far fewer members, because something free is worth nothing and gets treated that way. A small paid commitment, even twenty or thirty dollars, transforms the show rate and filters for people who actually intend to start.

Q: When should a gym advertise?
A: All year, with the budget weighted toward January and September but never concentrated there. A gym that acquires its entire year in the January rush faces a churn cliff in March with no pipeline behind it. Steady acquisition with seasonal peaks beats a single annual spike.

Q: What should a gym advertise, classes or membership?
A: Whichever one matches how you actually make money. A boutique studio sells the class experience and a specific instructor. A twenty-four hour access gym sells convenience and price. A personal training business sells a transformation and a person. Running one campaign for all three is why most gym ads say nothing.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RESIDENTIAL AND COMMERCIAL CLEANING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/house-cleaning-companies

One deep clean is a job. A biweekly recurring client is a business. Everything about how a cleaning company advertises should be aimed at the second one, and most of it is aimed at the first.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- The one-time deep clean is the most advertised and least valuable product in the trade. It has a real ticket and no future, and the lead cost has to be recovered in a single visit.
- Cleaning is a trust purchase before it is a price purchase. A stranger is getting a key to the house. Ads that lead with a rate and never show a human being are solving the wrong objection.
- Commercial and office cleaning is steadier, larger, and barely contested in the feed, and most residential cleaners never run a single campaign at it.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Recurring service as the headline offer, with a first-clean incentive that only unlocks on a recurring schedule.
- The team, the background checks, the insurance, and the guarantee made visible, because the real objection is who is in my house, not what does it cost.
- Instant online quoting from bedrooms, bathrooms, and square footage, so the lead gets a real number in the first minute instead of waiting for a callback.
- A separate commercial campaign aimed at offices, clinics, and property managers, where contracts are larger and the feed is nearly empty.
- Move-in and move-out campaigns timed to local listing activity, which is a reliable and underused source of high-ticket one-off work.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- One-time deep clean: $200 to $500
- Biweekly recurring client, annual: $2,500 to $5,000
- Commercial contract, monthly: $500 to $4,000
- What a recurring lead can cost: $30 to $80
- What the offer should be: The schedule, not the clean
Note: The same eighty dollar lead is a bad buy against a single deep clean and an outstanding buy against a client who stays on a biweekly schedule for two years.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for cleaning companies?
A: Yes, and the category is well suited to it because the decision is local, emotional, and trust-driven. The campaigns that fail are the ones advertising a one-time deep clean, which has to recover the entire lead cost in a single visit. Advertise the recurring schedule instead.

Q: How much does a house cleaning lead cost?
A: Thirty to eighty dollars in most markets. Against one deep clean that is uncomfortable. Against a biweekly client worth three thousand dollars a year for two years, it is very cheap. The offer in the ad determines which of those two you are actually buying.

Q: What is the best offer for a cleaning company ad?
A: A discount on the first clean that only applies when the customer starts a recurring schedule. It gives the ad a reason to act on, and it filters for the customer you want rather than the one-time bargain hunter who will never book again.

Q: How do you overcome the trust problem in cleaning ads?
A: Show the actual people. Background checks, insurance, a named guarantee, and real photographs of your team do more for conversion in this category than any price. The customer is handing a stranger a key to their home, and that is the objection the ad has to answer first.

Q: Should a cleaning company advertise to commercial clients?
A: Yes, and it is the most overlooked opportunity in the trade. Offices, medical suites, gyms, and property managers all buy recurring cleaning on contracts far larger than residential, and almost nobody is competing for their attention in the feed.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
HVAC COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/hvac-companies

HVAC advertising is not really about the tune-up. It is about owning the relationship with a homeowner whose system is eight years old, so that when it dies in July you are the number they already have.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- The emergency call is the worst customer you will ever have. They are panicked, they are price shopping three companies at once, and they will never call again. Every HVAC company built on emergency calls is starting from zero every summer.
- The tune-up offer is not a profit centre and was never supposed to be. It is a way to get a technician in front of an aging system. Companies that treat it as a margin product price it too high, advertise it badly, and get nothing.
- Replacement is where the money is and almost nobody advertises to it properly, because the trigger is invisible. You cannot see a fifteen-year-old furnace from the road. You can only reach it by being in front of that homeowner for months before it fails.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A seasonal tune-up offer, priced to get a tech through the door, running ahead of the season rather than during it. Cooling in April, heating in September.
- A maintenance plan pitched at the visit, not in the ad, because the plan is what turns one call into a decade of revenue.
- A separate replacement and financing campaign aimed at older homes, with monthly payment framing instead of a five-figure sticker.
- Retargeting everyone who has ever hit the site or watched the video, because the actual trigger is a failure you cannot schedule. When it happens you want to be the name already in their head.
- Emergency campaigns that switch on when the weather does, because bidding for emergency intent in mild weather is spending money on nothing.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- System replacement: $6,000 to $14,000
- Service or repair call: $150 to $700
- What a tune-up lead can cost: $20 to $60
- What a replacement lead can cost: $100 to $300
- The real asset: Maintenance plan members
Note: The tune-up campaign usually looks like it barely breaks even on its own. It is not supposed to. It is buying access to systems that will need replacing, and the replacement revenue is what makes the year.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for HVAC companies?
A: Yes, for tune-ups, maintenance plans, and replacement, which is most of the profit. They work poorly for true emergencies, where the homeowner searches Google with a broken system and buys in ten minutes. Run Meta to build the pipeline and to own the customer before the failure, and let search catch the panic calls.

Q: How much does an HVAC lead cost?
A: Twenty to sixty dollars for a tune-up lead, and one hundred to three hundred for a replacement lead. The tune-up looks better on a report and the replacement pays the bills. Judge them separately, because averaging them together hides which campaign is actually funding the business.

Q: Is a cheap tune-up offer worth running?
A: Yes, as long as you understand what you are buying. The tune-up is not a profit product. It is paid access to an aging system and a homeowner who now knows your technician by name. Companies that price it to make money on the visit get almost no takers and lose the replacement revenue behind it.

Q: When should HVAC ads run during the year?
A: Ahead of the season, not inside it. Cooling offers in April, heating offers in September. Advertising a tune-up in the first heat wave means competing with every emergency dollar in the market at the worst possible cost. The companies with full summer calendars booked them in spring.

Q: How do you sell system replacements with ads?
A: Separately, with monthly payment framing and a financing option stated up front. A five-figure number in an ad stops the scroll for the wrong reason. A monthly figure with a free load calculation or in-home estimate gets the appointment, and the appointment is where a replacement is actually sold.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
JUNK REMOVAL AND HAULING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/junk-removal-companies

Junk removal is the closest thing in the trades to an impulse purchase. Somebody looks at a garage on a Saturday morning and decides today is the day, and the company that can be there this afternoon wins.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- The decision is same-day and emotional, so a quote process that takes until Monday loses to anyone who answers the phone on Saturday.
- Pricing is opaque in this trade, which makes customers hesitate, and hesitation in an impulse category is a lost job.
- Commercial and property management work, evictions, foreclosures, construction cleanouts, office clearouts, is steadier and larger than residential and is almost never advertised to.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Same-day and next-day availability as the headline, because availability is the offer in this category.
- Visual pricing by load size, since a customer who can estimate their own cost in the ad is a customer who books.
- A separate commercial campaign for property managers, realtors, and contractors, which produces repeat accounts instead of one-off jobs.
- Radius targeting mapped to the routes you already run, so drive time stops eating the margin on a small ticket.
- Seasonal campaigns around spring cleaning, moves, and post-holiday, when the trigger is already in the customer's head.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Single item pickup: $100 to $250
- Full truckload: $400 to $900
- Commercial cleanout: $800 to $5,000
- What a lead can cost: $20 to $60
- What closes the job: Being available today
Note: Same-day capacity is worth more than any creative test in this category. If the honest answer is Tuesday, the ad should not promise today.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for junk removal?
A: Yes, and unusually well, because the trigger is visual and the decision is same-day. Somebody staring at a cluttered garage is exactly the person the feed reaches on a weekend morning. The company that can show up that afternoon takes most of that demand.

Q: How much does a junk removal lead cost?
A: Twenty to sixty dollars in most markets. Against a four hundred dollar truckload that is comfortable, and against a single item pickup it is tight. Route density and minimum ticket are what make the small jobs work rather than the lead price.

Q: Should junk removal ads show prices?
A: Yes, visually by load size. Opaque pricing creates hesitation, and hesitation kills an impulse purchase. A customer who can look at a graphic and estimate their own cost within fifty dollars is dramatically more likely to book than one who has to ask.

Q: Is commercial junk removal worth advertising?
A: It is usually the better half of the business. Property managers, realtors handling foreclosures, and contractors doing construction cleanouts book repeatedly, at larger tickets, on a schedule. Almost nobody is advertising to them, so the auction is cheap and the accounts last for years.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LANDSCAPING AND LAWN CARE COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/landscaping-and-lawn-care

There are two completely different businesses inside most landscaping companies: a recurring maintenance route, and design-build projects. They need different ads, different offers, and different definitions of a good lead.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Advertising mowing by the cut is the fastest way to a terrible year. A one-off mow at fifty dollars cannot carry a lead cost, and the customer disappears. The product being sold has to be the season or the route, not the visit.
- Design-build is where the margin is and it is sold on images. Most landscapers have hundreds of photos of finished work on their phone and run ads with none of them.
- Route density decides profitability in this trade and almost nobody targets for it. Ten customers on one street is a different business than ten customers across the county, and the ad radius is what determines which one you get.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Maintenance sold as a season or a monthly plan, never as a single cut, so a lead cost can be carried by more than one visit.
- Tight geographic targeting built around the routes you already run, so new customers land next to existing ones and drive time stops eating the margin.
- A separate design-build campaign carried by your own finished-project photography, with a real starting price so the leads arrive pre-qualified.
- Spring pre-booking that starts in late winter, because the companies with full spring calendars filled them in February.
- Off-season conversion into leaf removal, cleanups, holiday lighting, and hardscape, so the crew and the ad account both stay alive through winter.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Monthly maintenance plan: $120 to $400 per month
- Design-build project: $3,000 to $25,000
- What a maintenance lead can cost: $20 to $60
- What a design-build lead can cost: $60 to $200
- What actually decides profit: Route density
Note: A maintenance customer is worth the plan price times the months they stay, which is usually years. Judging a maintenance lead against a single month of revenue makes every campaign look unaffordable.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for lawn care companies?
A: Yes, when you sell the season rather than the cut. A single mow cannot carry a lead cost. A monthly plan that runs for two years absolutely can, and that difference is why two lawn companies can run identical ads with completely different outcomes.

Q: How much does a lawn care lead cost?
A: Twenty to sixty dollars for maintenance in most markets. That looks expensive against one mow and cheap against a customer who stays two seasons. Always measure against the lifetime of the plan, because that is what you are actually buying.

Q: When should landscaping ads start in the spring?
A: Six to eight weeks before the season, which usually means late winter. Homeowners decide on lawn care before the grass starts moving, and the companies with full spring routes booked them in February. Starting in April means bidding against everyone for what is left.

Q: How do you sell design-build landscaping with ads?
A: With your own finished-project photos and a stated starting price. Design-build is bought with the eyes, so stock imagery is useless. A real starting number filters out people expecting a thousand dollar backyard and leaves you with leads worth an appointment.

Q: What do landscapers advertise in winter?
A: Leaf removal and cleanups, holiday lighting where you offer it, hardscape and patio projects that get planned indoors, and early booking for spring maintenance at a locked rate. Switching the ads off in November and back on in March means rebuilding the account from cold every year.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MED SPAS AND AESTHETIC CLINICS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/med-spas

Med spa advertising is the most policy-restricted category a local business can run, and the most profitable when it is done inside the rules. The constraint is real. It is also why the operators who learn it have so little competition.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Meta treats aesthetics as a sensitive category. Before and after imagery, body-focused language, and anything implying the viewer has a personal problem will get an ad rejected and can get an account restricted. Most spa ads are written in exactly that voice.
- Discount-led acquisition builds the wrong list. A client acquired at seventy percent off returns at seventy percent off, and a med spa is a repeat business or it is nothing.
- The consult is the product and most spas advertise the treatment instead. Selling a syringe count in an ad skips the conversation where the actual package gets sold.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Copy and creative written against Meta's health and beauty policy from the first draft, so campaigns run instead of sitting in review, and the account stays healthy.
- The consultation as the offer, with a stated length, a named provider, and what the client walks out with. That is what sells the package, not a per-unit price.
- Treatment-specific campaigns, because injectables, laser, body contouring, and skin all have different buyers, different objections, and different seasons.
- Membership and package offers presented at the consult, since the entire economics of a med spa is repeat visits.
- Follow-up that runs for months. Aesthetic decisions are slow and private, and a lead that went quiet in March books in June if somebody stayed in touch.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- First treatment ticket: $300 to $900
- Annual value of a retained client: $2,000 to $6,000
- What a consult lead can cost: $40 to $120
- Consult show rate to defend: 70% or better
- Where the business is won: Rebooking, not acquisition
Note: Show rate is the number most spas never track and the one that decides everything. A hundred dollar lead that shows is cheaper than a forty dollar lead that does not.

QUESTIONS
Q: Can med spas advertise on Facebook?
A: Yes, inside Meta's health and beauty policy. What gets ads rejected is personal-attribute language that implies the viewer has a flaw, and before and after imagery used the wrong way. Written compliantly from the first draft, aesthetic campaigns run fine and face much less competition than the category deserves.

Q: Why do med spa ads get rejected?
A: Almost always for personal attributes. Copy addressed to the viewer's body, weight, age, or skin reads as implying a personal condition, which the policy forbids. The fix is writing about the treatment and the outcome in the third person rather than accusing the reader of a problem.

Q: How much does a med spa lead cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and twenty dollars for a consultation booking. That is only meaningful next to show rate and retained value. A retained client is worth thousands a year, so a hundred dollar consult lead that shows and rebooks is one of the better buys in local advertising.

Q: Should a med spa advertise discounts?
A: Rarely, and never as the main engine. A client acquired at a deep discount returns expecting one, and a med spa lives on repeat visits. A first-visit incentive attached to a package or membership works. A standalone half-price treatment builds a list that never becomes profitable.

Q: Can you use before and after photos in med spa ads?
A: Not the way most spas want to. Direct before and after comparisons in the ad creative are restricted under Meta's policy and are a common cause of rejections and account strikes. They belong on your own site and in the consult, where the platform's rules do not apply.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MOVING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/moving-companies

Moving is a dated purchase with a hard deadline and near-total commoditisation. The customer has one day circled on a calendar, they will get three quotes, and the first honest one usually wins.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Every mover looks identical in an ad: a truck, a box, a price per hour. Nothing in that creative gives a customer a reason to pick you.
- Quote speed decides this category. A customer who gets a real number in ten minutes rarely waits for the company that promised a callback tomorrow.
- The season is brutally compressed into summer, and companies that only advertise in season pay peak prices for jobs they were going to get anyway.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Instant or near-instant quoting from bedroom count, distance, and date, because whoever gives a real number first usually books the job.
- Transparent pricing, damage policy, and insurance stated plainly, which is the actual anxiety in a trade with a reputation problem.
- Long distance run as a separate campaign, since the ticket, the lead time, and the buyer are completely different from a local move.
- Off-season campaigns for corporate relocations, senior moves, and apartment turnovers, which keep the trucks moving in winter.
- Specialty positioning where you have it, whether pianos, art, seniors, or offices, because a specialist is not comparable on price.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Local move: $500 to $2,500
- Long distance move: $3,000 to $10,000
- What a local lead can cost: $30 to $90
- What a long distance lead can cost: $80 to $250
- What wins the booking: The first real quote
Note: Almost every moving lead is shopped against two or three competitors within the hour. Quote speed is worth more in this trade than any amount of creative testing.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for moving companies?
A: Yes, because moves are planned weeks ahead and the audience is targetable by life event. The constraint is response speed. Movers are shopped against two or three competitors in the first hour, and the company that supplies a real number first books a disproportionate share of the work.

Q: How much does a moving lead cost?
A: Thirty to ninety dollars for local and eighty to two hundred and fifty for long distance. Both work against the ticket. What breaks the maths is a slow quote, because a lead who has already booked someone else is a lead you paid full price for and never had.

Q: How do movers stand out from every other moving ad?
A: By being specific about the things customers are actually afraid of: damage policy, insurance, transparent pricing, and no surprise charges on the day. The trade has a reputation problem, and a company that addresses it directly stops being comparable on hourly rate alone.

Q: What do moving companies advertise in the off-season?
A: Corporate relocations, senior and downsizing moves, apartment turnovers, and storage. Summer demand arrives whether you advertise or not, and paying peak lead prices for it is the worst spend of the year. Winter is when the account should be building relationships and filling gaps.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PAINTING CONTRACTORS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/painting-contractors

Painting is a visual, high-ticket, seasonally swinging trade where the difference between a good year and a bad one is usually whether the schedule was booked before the season started.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Exterior work has a hard season and interior work does not, and most painting companies advertise as if they are one business, so winter is a cliff every single year.
- Free estimate ads produce enormous volume and a calendar full of unpaid driving, because nothing in the offer filters for scope or budget.
- Painting is bought with the eyes, and most painting ads show a roller and a tin instead of the finished room the customer is imagining.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Interior and exterior as separate campaigns on opposite seasonal schedules, so the business never has an empty quarter.
- Estimates qualified in the form: room count or square footage, interior or exterior, and timeline, so the site visit is worth the drive.
- Finished-room and finished-house photography as the entire creative direction, shot in homes that look like the target customer's home.
- Cabinet refinishing and specialty work run as their own campaign, since the margin is better and the buyer is different.
- Commercial and property management campaigns for repaint cycles, which are steady, repeatable, and barely advertised to.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Interior whole-house repaint: $3,000 to $9,000
- Exterior repaint: $4,000 to $12,000
- Cabinet refinishing: $2,500 to $6,000
- What a qualified lead can cost: $50 to $180
- What breaks most painters: Unqualified free estimates
Note: The real cost of a bad lead in this trade is the half day you spend driving to it. Qualify in the form, even at the cost of volume.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for painting contractors?
A: Yes, because painting is visual and the ticket is high enough to carry a real lead cost. The mistake is running a generic free estimate offer, which fills the calendar with unpaid site visits instead of jobs. Qualify scope and timeline in the form and the same budget performs completely differently.

Q: How much does a painting lead cost?
A: Fifty to one hundred and eighty dollars for a qualified lead. On a five thousand dollar interior repaint closing at one in three, that is very comfortable. The expensive lead is the cheap one that turns into a half day of driving for a job that was never real.

Q: How do painters stay busy in winter?
A: By running interior work as its own campaign on its own schedule. Interior repaints, cabinet refinishing, and trim work are indoor jobs with no weather constraint, and homeowners want them done before the holidays and in the slow months after. The companies that switch ads off in November create their own cliff.

Q: What should a painting ad show?
A: The finished room or the finished house, in a property that resembles the customer's. Rollers, tins, and crews in white overalls sell nothing, because the customer is not buying the process. They are buying an image of their own house that they already have in their head.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PEST CONTROL COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/pest-control-companies

Pest control is one of the best recurring-revenue businesses in the trades and it is almost always advertised as a one-off spray. That single framing decision is what caps most of these companies.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- A one-time treatment is a transaction. A quarterly plan is an annuity. Same truck, same technician, same chemical, and roughly eight times the customer value, and the ad usually sells the transaction.
- Demand is seasonal and pest-specific in a way that is completely predictable, and most companies run one flat campaign all year instead of moving with it.
- Termite and wildlife work carries the highest ticket in the trade and needs entirely different creative, but it gets buried inside the general pest campaign where it never gets tested.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- The recurring plan sold as the primary offer, with the one-time treatment positioned as the more expensive way to solve the same problem.
- Seasonal pest campaigns that move with the calendar: ants and termites in spring, mosquitoes in summer, rodents in autumn, spiders and roaches year round.
- Termite inspection and wildlife removal run separately, because the ticket, the urgency, and the buyer's fear are nothing like a general pest call.
- Neighbourhood targeting after any real infestation event, since pest problems cluster and the street that just called you has more customers on it.
- Retention as the growth engine. Plan cancellations are the single biggest hole in most pest control companies and cost nothing to fix compared with new acquisition.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- One-time treatment: $150 to $400
- Quarterly plan annual value: $400 to $900
- Termite treatment: $1,200 to $3,500
- What a plan lead can cost: $30 to $90
- The multiplier: Plan retention in years
Note: A ninety dollar lead looks bad against a one-time treatment and excellent against a plan a household keeps for four years. The offer you advertise decides which one you are buying.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for pest control?
A: Yes, especially for recurring plans and seasonal pests, where the homeowner has a visible problem and a short fuse. The campaigns that fail are the ones selling a one-time spray, because a single treatment cannot carry a lead cost the way a multi-year plan can.

Q: How much does a pest control lead cost?
A: Thirty to ninety dollars in most markets. Against a two hundred dollar one-time treatment that is tight. Against a quarterly plan worth six hundred a year for several years, it is one of the cheapest customer acquisitions in local service. Advertise the plan.

Q: Should pest control ads sell one-time treatments or plans?
A: Plans, with the one-time treatment offered as the more expensive alternative for the same problem. Selling the transaction caps your customer value at a single visit. Selling the plan turns identical work into recurring revenue and makes the whole advertising budget affordable.

Q: When is the best season for pest control advertising?
A: It shifts by pest rather than having one peak. Ants and termites in spring, mosquitoes through summer, rodents as it cools in autumn, roaches and spiders year round. Running one unchanged campaign across all of it means being irrelevant for most of the year.

Q: Is termite work worth advertising separately?
A: Yes. The ticket is far larger, the urgency is higher, and the emotional trigger is completely different from a general pest call. Buried inside a general campaign, termite creative never gets a fair budget or a fair test, which is why most companies assume it does not work.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PLUMBING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/plumbing-companies

Most plumbing marketing advice is about ranking for emergency searches. That is one narrow slice of the trade, it is the most expensive slice, and it is the one where the customer never calls you again.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Emergency intent belongs to search, and it is brutally priced. Trying to win burst pipe traffic in the Facebook feed is bidding on a moment that has not happened yet to someone who is not looking.
- The profitable plumbing work is planned: water heater replacement, repipes, water treatment, sewer line, fixture upgrades during a remodel. All of it is a considered purchase with a long window, and all of it is nearly invisible in most plumbers' advertising.
- Plumbers under-advertise the one thing they own that nobody else does, which is being inside the house. Every completed job is a chance at the next job and a review, and most of that value is left on the floor because nobody ever follows up.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Planned-work campaigns as the core: water heaters, repipes, filtration, sewer inspection. Long consideration, real ticket, and almost nobody else in the feed.
- A named diagnostic offer instead of a generic free estimate, because a bounded thing you can picture books far better than a vague favour.
- A database reactivation pass across every past customer you already have, which on most plumbing companies pays for the first two months of advertising by itself.
- Review generation wired into job completion, since a plumber's local search position is largely a function of recent reviews and nothing else.
- Emergency campaigns kept narrow and on standby, switched on for weather events rather than run all year at full price.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Water heater replacement: $1,200 to $3,500
- Repipe: $4,000 to $12,000
- Drain or service call: $150 to $600
- What a planned-work lead can cost: $40 to $150
- The free money: Your existing customer list
Note: Before a dollar of new spend, we look at how many past customers you have and when they were last contacted. In this trade that list is usually worth more than the first month of ads.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for plumbers?
A: For planned work, yes: water heaters, repipes, filtration, sewer work, remodel fixtures. For a burst pipe at midnight, no, because that customer is on Google with a wrench in their hand. Run Meta for the considered high-ticket jobs and let search have the emergencies.

Q: How much does a plumbing lead cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and fifty dollars for planned work in most markets. On a two thousand dollar water heater replacement that is comfortable math even at a one in three close rate. Emergency clicks on search cost far more and produce a customer who is unlikely to ever call you again.

Q: What should a plumber advertise if not emergencies?
A: The work with a real ticket and a decision window: water heater replacement, repipes, water treatment and filtration, sewer line inspection, and fixture upgrades during remodels. These have less competition in the feed, a bigger margin, and a customer who is choosing rather than panicking.

Q: Are reviews or ads more important for a plumbing company?
A: Reviews decide whether the ads work. A plumber with forty recent reviews and a plumber with four can run the same campaign and get wildly different results, because the homeowner checks before calling. Fix review generation first, then spend. It costs nothing and it changes every number downstream.

Q: What is the fastest way for a plumber to get jobs this month?
A: Contact every past customer. Most plumbing companies have hundreds of people who liked the work and have not heard from them since. A short, specific message about an inspection or a water heater approaching end of life typically books work within days, before a single ad has run.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
POOL SERVICE AND MAINTENANCE COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/pool-service-companies

A pool service company is a route business. The value of a new customer is not the first clean, it is the number of years they stay on your route, and every advertising decision should follow from that.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Weekly service is a small ticket with a long life, and advertising it as a one-off clean makes the lead cost look impossible when it is actually one of the best buys in local service.
- Equipment repair and replacement, pumps, heaters, filters, liners, is high ticket and nearly invisible in most pool companies' advertising.
- Route density decides whether this business makes money, and a customer twenty minutes off the route can be worth less than nothing.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Weekly and monthly service as the headline offer, with the lifetime of the route customer as the number you judge lead cost against.
- Radius targeting mapped to the routes you already run, so new customers land next to existing stops.
- A separate equipment repair and replacement campaign, which carries the ticket that funds the year.
- Opening and closing campaigns timed to the season, which are a reliable entry point onto the weekly route.
- Retention follow-up, because a route customer lost in year two costs more than several new acquisitions.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Weekly service, monthly: $120 to $300 per month
- Pool opening or closing: $250 to $600
- Equipment replacement: $800 to $5,000
- What a route lead can cost: $40 to $120
- What it is actually worth: Years on the route
Note: A hundred dollar lead that becomes a three-year route customer at two hundred a month is a four hundred dollar return on every dollar. That is the number to plan against, not the first invoice.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for pool service companies?
A: Yes, and the recurring structure makes the maths some of the friendliest in local service. A weekly service customer who stays three years is worth several thousand dollars, so a lead cost that looks alarming against one clean is trivial against the route.

Q: How much does a pool service lead cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and twenty dollars. Judge it against the lifetime of the route customer, not the first invoice. At two hundred dollars a month for three years, even a hundred and twenty dollar lead is one of the cheapest acquisitions you will ever make.

Q: Should pool companies advertise repairs separately?
A: Yes. Pumps, heaters, filters, and liners carry a far larger ticket than weekly service and have a different trigger, usually something that just broke. Running them inside the service campaign means they never get budget or a fair test.

Q: How does route density affect pool advertising?
A: It decides whether the work is profitable at all. A customer twenty minutes off your route can lose money on a normal service price. Target the radius around routes you already run, so every new customer is added to an existing stop rather than creating a new drive.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRESSURE WASHING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/pressure-washing-companies

I own Supreme Clean, a pressure washing company in Huntsville doing five thousand dollars a month. Every ad I would run for you, I have already paid for myself. This is the one page on this site where I am not describing a client's business. I am describing mine.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Pressure washing is an impulse-adjacent purchase with a visible trigger. Nobody wakes up wanting a clean driveway. They see a neighbour's house get done, or they list the house, or a guest is coming Saturday. The ad's job is to arrive at that moment and make booking take under sixty seconds.
- The trap is competing on price in a trade where the tool costs two thousand dollars and any teenager can buy one. The moment your ad leads with a number, you are in a race against a guy with a trailer and no insurance, and he will always be cheaper.
- The second trap is the quote form that takes three days. Half of the money in this trade is won by whoever answers first. Not whoever is best. Whoever answers first.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Before and after creative, shot on a phone, on real driveways in the actual neighbourhoods you want to work in. Generic stock washing footage does not convert here and never has.
- A single offer with a number attached to the outcome, not the hour. House wash, driveway, walkway, one price, booked for a named day.
