- A lead form that asks for four things: name, phone, address, what needs cleaning. Every extra field is money.
- An instant text back the second the form submits, before they close Facebook. Then a reminder at hour two and hour twenty-four if nobody has replied.
- Radius targeting on the neighbourhoods that actually pay, not the whole metro. A pressure washing ad shown ten miles past your drive time is a donation.

THE MATH I RUN ON MY OWN COMPANY (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Typical house wash ticket: $250 to $600
- Driveway or flatwork add-on: $100 to $250
- What a lead can cost and still work: $15 to $40
- Booking rate you need on those leads: 1 in 4 or better
- Where the season lives: March to October, front-loaded
Note: These are the numbers I plan against on my own business. Yours will differ by market and crew size, and we will find yours in the first thirty days of spend rather than guessing at them forever.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads actually work for pressure washing?
A: Yes, and it is one of the better trades for it, because the result is visual and the decision is fast. A before and after on a house that looks like the viewer's house does most of the selling. The failure mode is almost never the platform. It is a slow reply to the lead the ad produced.

Q: How much should a pressure washing lead cost?
A: In most markets, fifteen to forty dollars. On an average ticket of three hundred dollars and a one in four booking rate, a thirty dollar lead means about one hundred and twenty dollars of ad spend per booked job. That works. If leads cost eighty dollars, the offer or the creative is wrong, not the channel.

Q: What ad budget does a pressure washing company need to start?
A: Enough to buy roughly thirty leads a month, which in most markets is six hundred to one thousand dollars. Below that you cannot tell a bad campaign from a slow week, and you will kill something that was working. I will tell you the number for your market before you spend anything.

Q: Should the ad show a price?
A: It should show an outcome with a price attached, which is different. A number with no picture of what you get invites a price comparison you will lose. A specific package, for a specific kind of house, for a specific price, on a named day, is a different offer than a cheaper number from a guy with no insurance.

Q: Is winter dead for pressure washing ads?
A: Not dead, different. Residential demand drops and commercial demand does not. Off-season budget moves to gutter cleaning, commercial flatwork, holiday light installs where you offer it, and to filling the spring calendar early at a booked-now price. The worst winter move is switching the ads off entirely and rebuilding the account in March.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
REAL ESTATE AGENTS AND TEAMS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/real-estate-agents

Most agents buy buyer leads because they are cheap. Listings are where the business is, and seller leads are harder to get, slower to convert, and worth several times as much.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Cheap buyer leads are cheap because most of them are nine months from doing anything, and almost no agent has a follow-up system that survives nine months.
- Listings carry both sides of the commission and far less of the driving, and seller lead generation is a completely different campaign that most agents never run.
- Real estate is a special ad category on Meta with restricted targeting, so campaigns built on the usual demographic assumptions simply do not run.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Seller-first campaigns built on home valuation and market update offers, because that is the buyer of your time that actually pays.
- Follow-up measured in months with actual content, since a seller lead who is six months out is still the best lead you will get this week.
- Special ad category compliance from the first build, so campaigns run at all rather than being rejected for targeting.
- Local market authority content, since sellers pick the agent who clearly knows their street, not the one with the best headshot.
- Buyer campaigns kept as a secondary channel, sized to what your follow-up can actually carry rather than to what is cheap.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Average commission per side: $6,000 to $15,000
- What a seller lead can cost: $50 to $250
- What a buyer lead can cost: $10 to $40
- Follow-up window that pays: 6 to 12 months
- Where the business is: Listings
Note: A two hundred dollar seller lead that lists in eight months beats fifty ten dollar buyer leads that nobody called twice. This category rewards patience and a system more than any other.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for real estate agents?
A: Yes, particularly for seller lead generation, which is where the commission and the leverage are. Buyer leads are cheap and mostly long-horizon, so they only work for agents with a follow-up system that runs for months. Without one, cheap buyer leads are just a way to spend money.

Q: How much does a real estate seller lead cost?
A: Fifty to two hundred and fifty dollars, against a commission of several thousand. Even at the top of that range the maths works comfortably at a low conversion rate. Buyer leads cost ten to forty dollars and are worth exactly what your follow-up process makes them worth.

Q: What is the special ad category and how does it affect real estate ads?
A: Meta classifies housing ads as a special category, which removes most demographic and detailed targeting and restricts radius options. Campaigns built on standard targeting assumptions will not run. The build has to be designed around those limits from the start, using creative and geography to do the filtering.

Q: How long should you follow up with a real estate lead?
A: Six to twelve months, with real content rather than a check-in every week. Sellers move on their own timeline, and the agent who is still providing useful market information in month seven is the one who gets the listing appointment. Most agents quit in week two.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WATER, FIRE, AND MOLD RESTORATION COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/restoration-companies

Restoration is won in the first hour and sold through other people. The homeowner in a flooded basement calls whoever they were told to call, which means the advertising has two jobs: be first, and be the name the plumber already said.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- True emergency intent belongs to search and to the phone, not to the feed. A homeowner standing in water is not scrolling.
- Referral partners, plumbers, insurance agents, property managers, realtors, drive most of the volume in this trade, and almost nobody advertises to them.
- Demand is event-driven and unpredictable, and an ad account that has been switched off for two months cannot be scaled in the twelve hours that matter.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A standing storm and weather campaign kept warm all year so it can be scaled the same day an event hits the market.
- A referral partner campaign aimed at plumbers, agents, property managers, and realtors, which is the cheapest volume in the category and the least contested.
- Speed infrastructure: instant response, a real twenty-four hour line, and a stated arrival time you can keep.
- Insurance claim handling made explicit, since the homeowner's second question after how fast is who deals with the insurer.
- Mitigation and prevention campaigns during quiet periods, which keep the account active and the pipeline non-zero between events.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Water mitigation job: $3,000 to $15,000
- Fire or large loss: $20,000 to $100,000+
- What a qualified lead can cost: $100 to $400
- Referral partner value: Multiple jobs per year
- What wins the job: Arriving first
Note: The highest-return spend in this trade is usually not consumer advertising at all. It is being in front of the twenty plumbers and agents who decide where the next hundred jobs go.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for restoration companies?
A: Partly. They work well for referral partner acquisition, brand presence before an event, and storm response scaled the day weather hits. They work poorly for the emergency itself, because a homeowner with water rising is calling, not scrolling. The feed builds the pipeline, the phone catches the emergency.

Q: How do restoration companies get more referrals?
A: By advertising to the referrers. Plumbers, insurance agents, property managers, and realtors decide where a large share of restoration work goes, and almost nobody runs campaigns at them. It is the cheapest and least contested audience in the entire category.

Q: How much does a restoration lead cost?
A: One hundred to four hundred dollars for a qualified consumer lead. Against a five thousand dollar mitigation job that is fine, and against a large loss it is trivial. The real bargain is a referral partner who sends several jobs a year for a fraction of that.

Q: How do you prepare for storm season?
A: By keeping the account warm year round. A campaign that has been running steadily can be scaled within an hour of an event. One built from scratch after the storm spends its first days in the learning phase while every job in the market gets booked by someone else.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ROOFING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/roofing-companies

Roofing has the best ad math in home services and the worst lead handling. A single job pays for a month of advertising, which means the whole game is speed to contact and an honest inspection offer, not clever creative.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Roofing leads are expensive and that is fine. At a ten thousand dollar average job, a two hundred dollar lead is still cheap. The mistake is judging the channel on cost per lead instead of cost per signed contract.
- Roofing is the most lead-resold trade in America. The homeowner who filled in your form filled in four others in the same minute. If your first call happens the next morning, you are calling someone who already signed.
- Storm chasing works right up until it does not. A roofing company built only on storm response has no pipeline in a quiet year. The retail and replacement side has to be running the whole time for the business to survive a calm spring.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A free inspection offer with a real, bounded promise: what gets checked, how long it takes, and what you hand them at the end. Vague free inspections get vague leads.
- Speed first: an instant text the moment the form submits, a call attempt inside five minutes during business hours, and a defined sequence for the ones who do not pick up.
- Two campaigns running at once. Storm and insurance response, which spikes and dies, and retail replacement and repair, which is steady and pays the bills in a quiet year.
- Creative shot on your own roofs with your own crew, including the drone footage. Stock roofing photos read as a lead reseller, and homeowners have learned to recognise them.
- Qualification inside the form itself: roof age, own or rent, and what they noticed. Three questions cut the tire kickers without killing volume.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Average replacement job: $8,000 to $18,000
- Repair ticket: $400 to $1,500
- What a lead can cost and still work: $60 to $250
- Contracts per 10 inspections: 2 to 4, with fast contact
- The metric that decides it: Cost per signed contract
Note: Cost per lead is close to meaningless in roofing. A ninety dollar lead that never gets called back is worse than a two hundred and fifty dollar lead that gets called in four minutes.

QUESTIONS
Q: How much does a roofing lead cost on Facebook?
A: Sixty to two hundred and fifty dollars in most markets, and the high end is often the better buy. On a ten thousand dollar job at a one in four close rate, even a two hundred and fifty dollar lead means a thousand dollars of ad spend per signed contract. Judge the channel on contracts, not on lead price.

Q: Do Facebook ads work for roofing, or is Google better?
A: Both work and they do different jobs. Google catches the homeowner already searching, which is a smaller and more expensive pool. Facebook creates the demand: a homeowner who has been ignoring a stain on the ceiling sees a free inspection offer and finally acts. Most roofers should run Meta first because the volume is there and the cost per contract is usually lower.

Q: How fast do you have to call a roofing lead?
A: Minutes, not hours. Roofing leads are resold and shopped harder than any other trade, and the homeowner often submits several forms in one sitting. An automated text inside sixty seconds and a live call attempt inside five minutes roughly doubles what the same leads are worth.

Q: Should a roofing company advertise free inspections?
A: Yes, but a bounded one. Free inspection on its own attracts people with nothing wrong. Name what gets checked, how long you are on site, and what they get in their hand afterward, and you get a homeowner expecting a real conversation instead of a favour.

Q: What do roofers do for leads between storms?
A: Run the retail replacement and repair campaign the whole year, not just after weather. Aging roofs, discoloured shingles, and homes about to be listed are constant demand that has nothing to do with hail. Companies built purely on storm response have no pipeline in a quiet spring and lose their crews.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SALONS AND BARBERSHOPS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/salons-and-barbershops

A salon does not have a traffic problem, it has a rebooking problem. A client who comes eight times a year is worth ten of a client who came once on a discount and never returned.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Discount-led acquisition is endemic in this category and it buys exactly the client who leaves for the next discount, in a business that only works on repeats.
- The high-ticket services, colour, extensions, treatments, keratin, are where the margin is, and the ads are usually about haircuts.
- Stylists build personal followings and salons advertise the building, which wastes the strongest asset in the shop.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A first-visit offer tied to a rebooking, so the discount buys a relationship instead of a single appointment.
- High-ticket service campaigns run separately, because a colour correction client and a fifteen dollar cut client are not the same buyer.
- Stylist-led creative using real work from real chairs, with permission, since clients follow people and not premises.
- Online booking straight from the ad, because a direct message thread is where salon bookings go to die.
- Rebooking and recall built into the close of every appointment, which is worth more than any campaign in this category.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Cut: $25 to $80
- Colour or treatment: $120 to $400
- Annual value of a retained client: $500 to $2,000
- What a new client can cost: $15 to $50
- The number that decides it: Rebooking rate
Note: Acquisition is cheap in this category and retention is where everything is won or lost. If the rebooking rate is broken, more traffic makes the problem more expensive, not smaller.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook and Instagram ads work for salons?
A: Yes, and Instagram in particular, because the work is visual and the decision is local and personal. The reason salon ads disappoint is rarely the traffic. It is that the new client never rebooks, which turns every acquisition into a one-time transaction.

Q: How much should a salon pay for a new client?
A: Fifteen to fifty dollars, which is cheap against a client worth several hundred to a couple of thousand a year. That number is only good if rebooking works. Without it you are paying repeatedly for first visits that go nowhere.

Q: Should a salon run discount offers?
A: Only when the discount is attached to a rebooking or a package. A standalone half-price cut attracts the client who chases the next half-price cut elsewhere. Tie the offer to a second appointment and the same spend buys a relationship instead of a transaction.

Q: Should ads feature the salon or the stylists?
A: The stylists. Clients follow people, not premises, and a stylist's own work is the most persuasive creative available to the shop. Feature real work from real chairs with permission, and let each stylist's following do the work the building never could.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SIDING AND REPLACEMENT WINDOW COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/siding-and-window-companies

Siding and windows are sold in the living room, not in the feed. The only job the advertising has is to produce an in-home appointment with both decision makers present, and that is a much narrower target than a lead.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- A lead is worthless here. An appointment where one spouse is home and the other is not is close to worthless too, because the decision cannot be made in the room.
- These are five-figure purchases with a two to three month decision window, and most companies abandon follow-up inside two weeks.
- Energy savings claims are both the strongest angle and the fastest route to a policy problem or a complaint, because most of them are exaggerated in the industry as a matter of routine.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- The appointment as the conversion event, with confirmation steps designed to get both decision makers in the room.
- Financing and monthly payment framing up front, because a fifteen thousand dollar number in an ad stops the scroll for the wrong reason.
- Long follow-up sequences that run for months without becoming annoying, since the decision window genuinely is that long.
- Honest, checkable claims about efficiency and warranty, which protects the ad account and stands up when the homeowner verifies them.
- Neighbourhood-level targeting on housing stock age, because a fifteen-year-old subdivision is a completely different prospect from a new build.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Full siding job: $10,000 to $30,000
- Whole-home window replacement: $8,000 to $25,000
- What an appointment can cost: $150 to $500
- Sit-to-close rate to defend: 20% to 35%
- Decision window to plan for: 4 to 12 weeks
Note: Track cost per sit, not cost per lead. A campaign producing cheap leads and no appointments is the most expensive campaign you can run in this category.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for siding and window companies?
A: Yes, and they are one of the higher-ticket categories where the maths is forgiving. The discipline is optimising for in-home appointments rather than leads. Lead volume in this trade is easy to buy and almost entirely meaningless if nobody sits down at the kitchen table.

Q: How much should a window or siding appointment cost?
A: One hundred and fifty to five hundred dollars per set appointment. On a fifteen thousand dollar job closing at one in four sits, even five hundred dollars per appointment leaves the campaign comfortably profitable. The lead price is irrelevant next to the sit rate.

Q: Should the ad mention financing?
A: Yes, and early. A five-figure sticker price in a feed ad stops the scroll for the wrong reason. A monthly payment figure keeps the conversation alive long enough to get to an appointment, where the full number can be presented properly with the value attached to it.

Q: How long does it take to close a siding or window job?
A: Four to twelve weeks is normal, and it can be longer. That is why follow-up matters more than creative in this category. Companies that stop chasing at two weeks are abandoning most of their pipeline right before it was going to convert.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SOLAR INSTALLATION COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/solar-companies

Solar has the worst lead quality problem in local advertising. Anyone can fill in a form. Very few of those people own a suitable roof, pay a large enough bill, and can qualify for financing, and everything comes down to filtering for all three.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- An unqualified solar lead is not a cheap lead, it is a negative one. It burns a setter, a closer, and a site visit on someone who was never going to be installable.
- The category is saturated with door knockers, lead resellers, and exaggerated savings claims, so homeowners arrive already suspicious before you have said anything.
- Incentive and rate changes move the entire market, and campaigns written around a specific credit or rate go stale overnight and keep spending.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Qualification inside the form: ownership, average monthly bill, roof age and shading, and a credit band. Volume drops, closed deals go up.
- Honest savings framing with checkable numbers, which both protects the ad account and survives the homeowner verifying it later.
- Appointment setting as the conversion event, with confirmation steps aimed at getting both decision makers present.
- Creative built on local installs with real homeowners, because a national-looking solar ad reads as a lead reseller in a category full of them.
- Campaign copy reviewed whenever incentives or rates shift, so nothing keeps spending against an offer that no longer exists.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Residential install: $15,000 to $35,000
- What a qualified appointment can cost: $200 to $600
- Sit-to-close rate to defend: 15% to 30%
- Disqualification rate on raw leads: Often over half
- The metric that matters: Cost per closed install
Note: Cost per lead in solar is the most misleading number in local advertising. Track cost per qualified sit and cost per closed install, or the report will look excellent while the business loses money.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for solar companies?
A: Yes, but only with hard qualification built into the form. Solar generates lead volume effortlessly and most of it is unusable, because the homeowner rents, has a shaded or failing roof, or cannot finance. Filtered properly, Meta is one of the better solar channels. Unfiltered, it will quietly drain a budget.

Q: How much does a solar lead cost?
A: Raw leads can be cheap and are usually worthless. A qualified appointment costs two hundred to six hundred dollars, and on a twenty-five thousand dollar install closing at one in four sits, that is very workable. Never judge a solar campaign on cost per lead.

Q: How do you qualify solar leads?
A: Four questions: do they own the home, what is the average monthly electricity bill, how old is the roof and is it shaded, and roughly what credit band are they in. Each one cuts volume and raises close rate, and the combination is the difference between a profitable campaign and a treadmill.

Q: Why is solar lead quality so bad?
A: Because the offer is attractive to almost everyone and installable for a minority. The category is also crowded with resellers sending the same lead to several companies. If your form does not filter, you are buying the same unqualified homeowner that four competitors already called this morning.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TREE SERVICE AND ARBORIST COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/tree-service-companies

Tree work is two businesses in one truck: planned trimming, which is steady and cheap to advertise, and emergency removal, which is enormous, unpredictable, and won entirely on speed.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Emergency removal after a storm is the highest-ticket work in the trade and it is won in the first hour. A company that is not already live in the ad account when the storm hits cannot get there in time.
- Planned trimming and pruning is a much softer decision with a much longer window, and running it in the same campaign as emergency work confuses both.
- Tree work carries the highest liability fear of any home service. Insurance and certification are the actual objection, and they are usually a footnote in the ad instead of the headline.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- A standing storm-response campaign that can be switched on within minutes and targeted at the neighbourhoods that were actually hit.
- A separate planned-work campaign for trimming, pruning, and health assessments, running steadily all year.
- Insurance, certification, and licensing in the headline, because a homeowner picturing a tree through their roof is buying safety, not price.
- Before and after creative on large removals, which is the most compelling imagery in the trade and the most underused.
- Stump grinding and cleanup positioned as an add-on inside the ad, raising the ticket on work already on the calendar.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Large tree removal: $800 to $4,000
- Trimming and pruning: $300 to $1,200
- Emergency storm removal: $1,500 to $8,000
- What a lead can cost: $40 to $150
- What decides storm revenue: Minutes, not marketing
Note: An account that has been running steadily is one you can scale in twenty minutes when weather hits. An account that has been off for three months is not, and that gap is where a storm season is won or lost.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for tree service companies?
A: Yes, for both planned trimming and storm response, though they behave completely differently. Planned work is a steady, low-cost campaign. Storm work is a standing campaign you scale within minutes of weather, and it is the most profitable advertising in the trade when the account is already warm.

Q: How much does a tree service lead cost?
A: Forty to one hundred and fifty dollars. Against an eight hundred dollar trim that is workable, and against a three thousand dollar removal it is cheap. Storm leads cost more and convert faster, because the homeowner has a tree on the garage and is not shopping around.

Q: How do you advertise after a storm?
A: By scaling a campaign that was already running, targeted to the neighbourhoods that were actually hit. Building a new campaign from scratch after the storm means waiting through the learning phase while the work gets booked by somebody else. The preparation is what earns the storm revenue.

Q: What do homeowners actually care about when hiring a tree company?
A: Whether you are insured and whether your crew will drop a limb through the roof. Certification, licensing, and liability coverage belong in the headline of the ad, not in fine print. Price is a distant second when a sixty foot oak is leaning over a bedroom.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VETERINARY CLINICS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/veterinary-clinics

A new veterinary client is not a visit. It is ten to fifteen years of an animal's life, which makes it one of the highest lifetime values in any local business, and almost nobody advertises like it.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Vet practices advertise discounted vaccinations and first exams, which buys price shoppers into a category where price shoppers are the least loyal clients you can have.
- The highest-value moment in the entire relationship is a new puppy or kitten, and it is one of the most targetable audiences in local advertising, and it goes almost entirely uncontested.
- Wellness plans are the closest thing a practice has to recurring revenue, and most of them are never advertised at all.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- New pet campaigns aimed at puppy and kitten owners, which is where a fifteen year relationship starts and where the competition is thinnest.
- Wellness plans as the offer rather than a discounted single visit, because the plan is what makes the client value real.
- Warmth and the actual team as the creative, since choosing a vet is an emotional decision about who you trust with a family member.
- Specialty and capability campaigns for dentistry, surgery, exotics, or emergency capacity, which differentiate you from every other clinic in town.
- Reminder and recall systems treated as marketing, because a lapsed client is far cheaper to recover than a new one is to buy.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Annual spend per pet: $500 to $1,500
- Lifetime client value: $6,000 to $20,000
- What a new client can cost: $40 to $150
- Wellness plan, monthly: $40 to $120 per month
- The best audience in the category: New puppy and kitten owners
Note: At a lifetime value in the thousands, a hundred dollar new client is one of the cheapest acquisitions in local business. The reason vet marketing underperforms is almost never the price of the lead.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for veterinary clinics?
A: Yes, and the economics are unusually strong because a new client represents a decade or more of care. Choosing a vet is an emotional trust decision, which the feed handles far better than a search result, and new pet owners are one of the easiest audiences to reach.

Q: How much should a vet clinic pay for a new client?
A: Forty to one hundred and fifty dollars is very reasonable against a lifetime value in the thousands. Most clinics dramatically underspend because they are measuring against the first visit instead of against the years of care that follow it.

Q: What is the best audience for a veterinary practice?
A: New puppy and kitten owners. That household is choosing a vet for the next ten to fifteen years, they are choosing right now, and almost nobody is competing for their attention. It is the single most valuable and most neglected audience in the category.

Q: Should vets advertise discounts?
A: Rarely. Discounted vaccinations attract price-driven clients in a category where loyalty is the entire business model. Advertise a wellness plan, a new pet package, or the practice itself instead, and you acquire the client who stays for the life of the animal.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WINDOW CLEANING COMPANIES
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/window-cleaning-companies

Window cleaning has the tightest margins and the best recurring structure in exterior services. Whether it is a good business or a hard one comes down to route density and whether the customer is on a schedule.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- A one-off residential window clean is a small ticket carrying a full drive time. Advertise that alone and the math never gets comfortable, no matter how cheap the leads are.
- The recurring commercial route, storefronts, offices, restaurants, is where this trade becomes an actual business, and almost nobody advertises to it because everyone is chasing homeowners.
- Window cleaning is the easiest service in the world to bundle and the least bundled. The same visit could carry gutter cleaning, screen repair, and a house wash.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Recurring schedules as the offer: twice a year residential, monthly or quarterly commercial, with a price that rewards staying on the calendar.
- Bundled packages built into the ad, since adding gutters or a house wash to an existing stop raises the ticket without adding drive time.
- A separate commercial campaign for storefronts, offices, and restaurants, where contracts are recurring and the feed is empty.
- Radius targeting built around the routes you already run, because in this trade drive time is the real cost of every job.
- Seasonal timing around spring cleaning and pre-holiday, when residential demand actually spikes.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Residential window clean: $150 to $400
- Commercial storefront, monthly: $80 to $400 per month
- What a residential lead can cost: $15 to $40
- What a commercial lead can cost: $40 to $120
- What decides the margin: Drive time per stop
Note: Price drive time into every job before deciding what a lead can cost. Two jobs on the same street is a different business from two jobs twenty minutes apart.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for window cleaning?
A: Yes, when the offer is a recurring schedule or a bundle rather than a single clean. A one-off residential job carries a small ticket and a full drive time, so it struggles to absorb a lead cost. A twice-yearly schedule or a bundled exterior package absorbs it easily.

Q: How much does a window cleaning lead cost?
A: Fifteen to forty dollars residential, forty to one hundred and twenty commercial. The commercial lead looks expensive and is usually the better buy, because a storefront on a monthly schedule is worth several thousand dollars a year and stays for years.

Q: Should window cleaners go after commercial or residential?
A: Both, in separate campaigns. Residential gives you volume and cash flow. Commercial gives you recurring revenue, predictable routes, and almost no competition in the feed. Most window cleaning companies run only the residential half and wonder why the year is lumpy.

Q: What should a window cleaner bundle with a clean?
A: Gutter cleaning, screen repair, and a house wash. The truck is already there and the drive time is already paid for, so every add-on is close to pure margin. Bundling in the ad itself raises the average ticket before the customer ever speaks to you.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WINDOW TINT AND PAINT PROTECTION SHOPS
URL: https://tothemax.marketing/for/window-tint-shops

Tint is one of the few local trades where the customer already knows what they want before they search. They are not deciding whether to tint. They are deciding whose bay their car sits in. That changes what the ad has to do.

WHAT GOES WRONG
- Every tint shop in the city is running the same ad: a dark sedan, a price, and the word ceramic. When the creative is identical, the only variable left is the number, and the shop with the worst film wins the click.
- The high-margin work, full-front PPF, full-vehicle wraps, ceramic coating packages, does not sell from a price ad. It sells from a specific film brand, a named warranty, and an install bay a person can see. Most shops never show any of it.
- Tint has a second buyer nobody advertises to: the dealership, the fleet manager, and the home and storefront owner. Same film, same crew, much bigger ticket, almost zero competition in the feed.

WHAT TO THE MAX BUILDS
- Creative that shows the bay, the crew, and the film brand you actually carry, because the buyer at the top of the market is buying the installer, not the tint.
- The offer built on the package, not the discount: film tier, warranty length, turnaround time, and a booked slot.
- Split campaigns by ticket size. Standard tint and full PPF are two different businesses, and running them in one campaign makes the cheap one eat the budget.
- A booking flow that captures the vehicle year, make, and model up front, so your quote in the reply text is a real number instead of another question.
- A second campaign aimed at commercial and residential flat glass, where the competition in the feed is close to nothing and the ticket is often larger.

THE MATH TO RUN BEFORE YOU SPEND (planning ranges and targets, not claimed results)
- Full vehicle ceramic tint: $400 to $900
- Full-front PPF: $1,200 to $2,500
- What a lead can cost and still work: $25 to $70
- Booking rate on a warm tint lead: 1 in 3 is achievable
- Where the margin actually lives: PPF, coatings, commercial flat glass
Note: Ranges vary hard by market and film line. We set your real targets from your own closed jobs in the first month, not from a benchmark chart.

QUESTIONS
Q: Do Facebook ads work for window tint shops?
A: Yes, and better than most trades, because the buyer is usually already sold on tinting and is only choosing a shop. The ad does not have to create demand. It has to show a bay, a film line, and a warranty that makes you the obvious choice, then make booking one tap.

Q: How much does a window tint lead cost?
A: Twenty-five to seventy dollars in most markets, and the spread is mostly about ticket size. A standard tint lead at the low end and a PPF lead at the high end are both good buys. What breaks the math is running them in the same campaign, where the cheap leads take the budget.

Q: Should a tint shop advertise a price or a package?
A: A package. Price ads in tint are a race to the bottom against shops using film that fails in two years. A named film line, a stated warranty, a turnaround time, and a photo of your own bay sells against a cheaper number, because it changes what the customer thinks they are buying.

Q: How do you sell PPF and ceramic coating, not just cheap tint?
A: You run them as a separate campaign, with separate creative, aimed at newer and higher-value vehicles. PPF buyers respond to protection and resale value, not to darkness and heat rejection. Mixed into a tint campaign, PPF creative loses every auction to the cheaper offer and never gets a fair test.

Q: Can a tint shop get commercial work from Facebook ads?
A: Yes, and it is the most underpriced thing in the trade. Office buildings, storefronts, and homeowners with west-facing glass all buy film, and almost nobody is advertising to them. Same crew, same film, higher ticket, and an auction with far fewer bidders in it.
